title: Trump lashes out at Albanese government over new social media laws
text:
By DAILY MAIL

Published:  09:31 AEST, 9 September 2026   |  Updated:  07:46 AEST, 23 September 2026

232

View  comments

Donald Trump has lashed out at Anthony Albanese's government over proposed laws that could hit major US tech companies with fines of up to $100million and force social media platforms to let users opt out of algorithm-driven feeds.

Under the Albanese government's proposed digital duty of care, social media companies would have to meet minimum safety standards and give users a choice between algorithm-selected content and a feed made up only of posts from people they follow.

Platforms would also be required to take steps to protect users from harmful content.

That could include material promoting eating disorders, misogynistic content, pornography or the glorification of crime.

Companies that fail to comply with the duty of care could face fines of up to $100million.

The changes would build on Australia's world-first social media ban for children under 16.

A White House spokesman said the Trump administration had repeatedly warned countries against measures targeting American technology companies in a statement issued on Wednesday morning.

'President Trump has unequivocally warned trading partners against imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America's leading technology sector. The [Trump] administration remains committed to raising these issues with our trading partners,' the spokesman said.

Donald Trump has lashed out at Anthony Albanese's government over proposed social media laws that could expose major US tech companies to fines of up to $100million

Under the proposed My Feed, My Way initiative, social media platforms would be required to let users opt out of algorithm-driven feeds and choose more of what they see online

Meanwhile, members of the Opposition and One Nation have labelled the proposal an overreach, criticising provisions in the draft laws that would give the communications minister power to determine what is classified as harmful content online.

Governments should not have the power to control social media content, Nationals leader Matt Canavan said.

'People should be able to freely express their views, and any attempt to silence or gag or influence those by governments should be absolutely rejected in a free and open democratic society,' Senator Canavan said.

Opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said it was an attempt to 'censor' the internet.

Albanese rejected the claim, saying 'it's about giving people control themselves over what they see'.

How the laws will work?

Under the draft legislation, social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and TikTok must give users an option of whether they want their default feed to include personalised content recommended by an algorithm or only content from their friends and people they follow. This option will appear as a popup box for people when they use social media.

The draft bill also requires digital service providers to protect all users from seriously harmful material and conduct, including illegal content.

This includes content relating to child sexual exploitation and child sexual abuse, grooming, promoting or inciting sexual violence, supporting terrorism, and encouraging criminal offences, illicit drug use and abhorrent violent conduct.

In addition, digital service providers must also protect teenagers and children from addictive features and harmful content.

This includes pornography and content that encourages disordered eating, hostile attitudes towards women and gender equality, dangerous stunts, and harassment or bullying.

Companies must also conduct regular risk assessments which identify 'all reasonably foreseeable risks', as well as the content and design features that give rise to those risks.

They must make these assessments available to the eSafety Commissioner within 30 days, if requested.

The draft bill also empowers the commissioner to issue removal notices for 'nudify' apps and websites, and streamline the child cyberbullying and adult cyber abuse schemes.

Source: The Conversation
